    • p3.1 [757–854] Nashville's founding in 1779 by James Robertson and John Donelson was tied directly to the river.

    • p3.3 [992–1077] The settlement grew on the bluff above the river because the river was the only road.
▸ p4 [1079–1371]  ← no shared name with p3: a transition must be written
    • p4.1 [1079–1203] Steamboats reached Nashville in 1819, and the river became the city's link to the cotton and tobacco markets of New Orleans.
    • p4.2 [1204–1287] By the 1850s Nashville was a major river port, and warehouses lined the waterfront.
    • p4.3 [1288–1371] Cotton, tobacco, iron, and lumber moved downriver; manufactured goods came back up.
▸ p5 [1373–1630]  ← no shared name with p4: a transition must be written
    • p5.1 [1373–1403] The river also brought danger.
    • p5.2 [1404–1451] The flood of 1927 covered much of the low city.
    • p5.3 [1452–1630] The flood of May 2010 crested at 51.86 feet, put the Opryland area and the downtown riverfront under water, and caused more than two billion dollars in damage in Nashville alone.
▸ p6 [1632–1966]  ← no shared name with p5: a transition must be written
    • p6.1 [1632–1739] The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers built a system of locks and dams on the Cumberland beginning in the 1920s.
    • p6.2 [1740–1799] Wolf Creek Dam, completed in 1951, created Lake Cumberland.
    • p6.3 [1800–1966] Old Hickory Dam, completed in 1954, created Old Hickory Lake just upstream of Nashville, and Cheatham Dam below the city regulates the river's level through downtown.
▸ p7 [1968–2262]  ← no shared name with p6: a transition must be written
    • p7.1 [1968–2050] Today the Port of Nashville handles barge traffic in aggregates, grain, and steel.
    • p7.2 [2051–2095] The riverfront has been rebuilt as parkland.
    • p7.3 [2096–2208] Cumberland Park, the pedestrian bridge, and the Ascend Amphitheater sit on the banks where the warehouses stood.
    • p7.4 [2209–2262] The river remains the reason the city is where it is.
▸ p8 [2265–2341]  ← no shared name with p7: a transition must be written
    • p8.1 [2265–2341] How Did the Cumberland River Enable Nashville’s Founding and Early Survival?
▸ p9 [2343–2745]  ← no shared name with p8: a transition must be written
    • p9.1 [2343–2515] James Robertson’s party arrived at the future Nashville site on Christmas Eve 1779 because the Cumberland offered the only practical route into Middle Tennessee’s interior.
    • p9.2 [2516–2585] The river’s westward flow toward the Ohio provided a two-way highway.
    • p9.3 [2586–2745] Flatboats floated supplies downstream from eastern settlements; keelboat crews poled their way back upstream with trade goods, establishing a two-way exchange.
▸ p10 [2747–2828]  ← no shared name with p9: a transition must be written
    • p10.1 [2747–2828] What Role Did the Cumberland Play During Nashville’s Steamboat and Civil War Era?
▸ p11 [2830–3418]  ← no shared name with p10: a transition must be written
    • p11.1 [2830–3017] That strategic transport position made Nashville a military prize during the Civil War. Union forces captured the city in February 1862 specifically to control Cumberland River logistics.
    • p11.2 [3018–3126] Federal gunboats and supply steamers moved 15,000 troops and their equipment upriver from Paducah in a week.
    • p11.3 [3127–3206] That concentration of force would have been impossible over muddy winter roads.
    • p11.4 [3207–3418] Nashville remained a Union garrison and supply depot through 1865, with the river delivering rations, ammunition, and reinforcements that sustained Sherman’s Atlanta campaign and Thomas’s Army of the Cumberland.
▸ p12 [3420–3700]  ← takes up "federal" from p11
    • p12.1 [3420–3514] Confederate forces never retook the city partly because they couldn’t interdict river traffic.
    • p12.2 [3515–3700] Federal gunboats patrolled the Cumberland from its mouth to Carthage, 60 miles upstream from Nashville, keeping the supply line open even when Confederate cavalry raided the rail lines.
▸ p13 [3702–4221]  ← takes up "cumberland" from p12
    • p13.1 [3702–3846] Those disasters prompted the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to build the system of locks, dams, and reservoirs that now regulates Cumberland flow.
    • p13.2 [3847–4018] Old Hickory Dam (completed 1954) and J. Percy Priest Dam (1968) upstream from Nashville ended seasonal flooding and maintained a year-round navigation channel 9 feet deep.
    • p13.3 [4019–4221] The regulated river enabled modern development along the East Bank, including the sports stadium district, Nissan Stadium, and the marinas where corporate cruises and private event charters now operate.
▸ p14 [4223–4555]  ← no shared name with p13: a transition must be written
    • p14.1 [4223–4299] What made the Cumberland River strategically important during the Civil War?
    • p14.2 [4300–4422] The river allowed Union forces to move 15,000 troops and equipment from Paducah to Nashville in one week in February 1862.
    • p14.3 [4423–4555] Federal control of the waterway kept supply lines open to Nashville’s garrison even when Confederate cavalry disrupted rail service.
▸ p15 [4557–4832]  ← takes up "civil war" from p14
    • p15.1 [4557–4687] Entertainment has replaced commerce on the Cumberland, but tourists and locals now experience the same river that built Nashville.
    • p15.2 [4688–4832] The bedrock channel that floated Fort Nashborough’s supply flatboats and Civil War gunboats now carries modern pontoon vessels past the skyline.
